subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
stem: Given \(\tan \text{A} = \dfrac{4}{3}\), find the other trigonometric ratios of the angle A.
solution:
Let us first draw a right triangle ABC.

We know that \(\tan \text{A} = \dfrac{\text{BC}}{\text{AB}} = \dfrac{4}{3}\).

Therefore, if BC \(= 4k\), then AB \(= 3k\), where \(k\) is a positive number.

By the Pythagoras Theorem, \(\text{AC}^2 = \text{AB}^2 + \text{BC}^2 = (4k)^2 + (3k)^2 = 25k^2\), so AC \(= 5k\).

Now we can write all the trigonometric ratios using their definitions:

\(\sin \text{A} = \dfrac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} = \dfrac{4k}{5k} = \dfrac{4}{5}\),  \(\cos \text{A} = \dfrac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}} = \dfrac{3k}{5k} = \dfrac{3}{5}\)

Therefore, \(\cot \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{\tan \text{A}} = \dfrac{3}{4}\), \(\operatorname{cosec} \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{\sin \text{A}} = \dfrac{5}{4}\) and \(\sec \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{\cos \text{A}} = \dfrac{5}{3}\).

subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
stem: If \(\angle\)B and \(\angle\)Q are acute angles such that \(\sin \text{B} = \sin \text{Q}\), then prove that \(\angle\)B \(=\) \(\angle\)Q.
solution:
Let us consider two right triangles ABC and PQR where \(\sin \text{B} = \sin \text{Q}\).

We have \(\sin \text{B} = \dfrac{\text{AC}}{\text{AB}}\) and \(\sin \text{Q} = \dfrac{\text{PR}}{\text{PQ}}\).

Then \(\dfrac{\text{AC}}{\text{AB}} = \dfrac{\text{PR}}{\text{PQ}}\).

Therefore, \(\dfrac{\text{AC}}{\text{PR}} = \dfrac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = k\), say.  ... (1)

Now, using Pythagoras Theorem,

\(\text{BC} = \sqrt{\text{AB}^2 - \text{AC}^2}\) and \(\text{QR} = \sqrt{\text{PQ}^2 - \text{PR}^2}\).

So, \(\dfrac{\text{BC}}{\text{QR}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{\text{AB}^2 - \text{AC}^2}}{\sqrt{\text{PQ}^2 - \text{PR}^2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{k^2\text{PQ}^2 - k^2\text{PR}^2}}{\sqrt{\text{PQ}^2 - \text{PR}^2}} = k\)  ... (2)

From (1) and (2), \(\dfrac{\text{AC}}{\text{PR}} = \dfrac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \dfrac{\text{BC}}{\text{QR}}\).

Then, by the SSS similarity criterion, \(\triangle\)ACB \(\sim\) \(\triangle\)PRQ, and therefore \(\angle\)B \(=\) \(\angle\)Q.

subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
stem: In a right triangle ABC, right-angled at B, if \(\tan \text{A} = 1\), then verify that \(2 \sin \text{A} \cos \text{A} = 1\).
solution:
In \(\triangle\)ABC, \(\tan \text{A} = \dfrac{\text{BC}}{\text{AB}} = 1\), i.e., BC \(=\) AB.

Let AB \(=\) BC \(= k\), where \(k\) is a positive number.

Now, \(\text{AC} = \sqrt{\text{AB}^2 + \text{BC}^2} = \sqrt{(k)^2 + (k)^2} = k\sqrt{2}\).

Therefore, \(\sin \text{A} = \dfrac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(\cos \text{A} = \dfrac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

So, \(2 \sin \text{A} \cos \text{A} = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 1\), which is the required value.

subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
stem: In \(\triangle\)OPQ, right-angled at P, OP \(= 7\) cm and OQ \(-\) PQ \(= 1\) cm (see Fig. 8.12). Determine the values of \(\sin \text{Q}\) and \(\cos \text{Q}\).
solution:
In \(\triangle\)OPQ, we have \(\text{OQ}^2 = \text{OP}^2 + \text{PQ}^2\),

i.e., \((1 + \text{PQ})^2 = \text{OP}^2 + \text{PQ}^2\)  (since OQ \(=\) 1 \(+\) PQ)

i.e., \(1 + \text{PQ}^2 + 2\text{PQ} = \text{OP}^2 + \text{PQ}^2\)

i.e., \(1 + 2\text{PQ} = 7^2\)  (since OP \(= 7\) cm)

i.e., \(\text{PQ} = 24\) cm and \(\text{OQ} = 1 + \text{PQ} = 25\) cm.

So, \(\sin \text{Q} = \dfrac{\text{OP}}{\text{OQ}} = \dfrac{7}{25}\) and \(\cos \text{Q} = \dfrac{\text{PQ}}{\text{OQ}} = \dfrac{24}{25}\).

stem: In \(\triangle\)ABC, right-angled at B, AB \(= 5\) cm and \(\angle\)ACB \(= 30^\circ\) (see Fig. 8.19). Determine the lengths of the sides BC and AC.
solution:
To find the length of the side BC, we choose the trigonometric ratio involving BC and the given side AB. Since BC is the side adjacent to angle C and AB is the side opposite to angle C,

\(\dfrac{\text{AB}}{\text{BC}} = \tan \text{C}\)

i.e., \(\dfrac{5}{\text{BC}} = \tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), which gives \(\text{BC} = 5\sqrt{3}\) cm.

To find AC, we consider \(\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}}\),

i.e., \(\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{5}{\text{AC}}\), i.e., \(\text{AC} = 10\) cm.

Note that alternatively we could have used the Pythagoras theorem: \(\text{AC} = \sqrt{\text{AB}^2 + \text{BC}^2} = \sqrt{5^2 + (5\sqrt{3})^2} = 10\) cm.

stem: In \(\triangle\)PQR, right-angled at Q (see Fig. 8.20), PQ \(= 3\) cm and PR \(= 6\) cm. Determine \(\angle\)QPR and \(\angle\)PRQ.
solution:
Given PQ \(= 3\) cm and PR \(= 6\) cm.

Therefore, \(\dfrac{\text{PQ}}{\text{PR}} = \sin \text{R}\),

i.e., \(\sin \text{R} = \dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

So, \(\angle\)PRQ \(= 30^\circ\).

And therefore, \(\angle\)QPR \(= 60^\circ\)  (since the three angles of a triangle add to \(180^\circ\) and \(\angle\)Q \(= 90^\circ\)).

Since \(\sin(\text{A} - \text{B}) = \dfrac{1}{2}\), therefore \(\text{A} - \text{B} = 30^\circ\)  ... (1)

Also, since \(\cos(\text{A} + \text{B}) = \dfrac{1}{2}\), therefore \(\text{A} + \text{B} = 60^\circ\)  ... (2)

Solving (1) and (2), we get \(\text{A} = 45^\circ\) and \(\text{B} = 15^\circ\).

stem: Express the ratios \(\cos \text{A}\), \(\tan \text{A}\) and \(\sec \text{A}\) in terms of \(\sin \text{A}\).
solution:
Since \(\cos^2 \text{A} + \sin^2 \text{A} = 1\), therefore \(\cos^2 \text{A} = 1 - \sin^2 \text{A}\),

i.e., \(\cos \text{A} = \pm\sqrt{1 - \sin^2 \text{A}}\).

This gives \(\cos \text{A} = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 \text{A}}\)  (since \(\cos \text{A}\) is positive for an acute angle A).

Hence, \(\tan \text{A} = \dfrac{\sin \text{A}}{\cos \text{A}} = \dfrac{\sin \text{A}}{\sqrt{1 - \sin^2 \text{A}}}\)

and \(\sec \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{\cos \text{A}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \sin^2 \text{A}}}\).

LHS \(= \sec \text{A}\,(1 - \sin \text{A})(\sec \text{A} + \tan \text{A})\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{\cos \text{A}}(1 - \sin \text{A})\left(\dfrac{1}{\cos \text{A}} + \dfrac{\sin \text{A}}{\cos \text{A}}\right)\)

\(= \dfrac{(1 - \sin \text{A})(1 + \sin \text{A})}{\cos^2 \text{A}} = \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 \text{A}}{\cos^2 \text{A}}\)

\(= \dfrac{\cos^2 \text{A}}{\cos^2 \text{A}} = 1 = \) RHS

LHS \(= \dfrac{\cot \text{A} - \cos \text{A}}{\cot \text{A} + \cos \text{A}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\cos \text{A}}{\sin \text{A}} - \cos \text{A}}{\dfrac{\cos \text{A}}{\sin \text{A}} + \cos \text{A}}\)

\(= \dfrac{\cos \text{A}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin \text{A}} - 1\right)}{\cos \text{A}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin \text{A}} + 1\right)} = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{\sin \text{A}} - 1}{\dfrac{1}{\sin \text{A}} + 1}\)

\(= \dfrac{\operatorname{cosec} \text{A} - 1}{\operatorname{cosec} \text{A} + 1} = \) RHS

Since we will apply the identity involving \(\sec\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\), let us first convert the LHS into terms of \(\sec\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\) by dividing numerator and denominator by \(\cos\theta\):

LHS \(= \dfrac{\sin\theta - \cos\theta + 1}{\sin\theta + \cos\theta - 1} = \dfrac{\tan\theta - 1 + \sec\theta}{\tan\theta + 1 - \sec\theta}\)

\(= \dfrac{(\tan\theta + \sec\theta) - 1}{(\tan\theta - \sec\theta) + 1} = \dfrac{\{(\tan\theta + \sec\theta) - 1\}(\tan\theta - \sec\theta)}{\{(\tan\theta - \sec\theta) + 1\}(\tan\theta - \sec\theta)}\)

\(= \dfrac{(\tan^2\theta - \sec^2\theta) - (\tan\theta - \sec\theta)}{\{\tan\theta - \sec\theta + 1\}(\tan\theta - \sec\theta)}\)

\(= \dfrac{-1 - \tan\theta + \sec\theta}{(\tan\theta - \sec\theta + 1)(\tan\theta - \sec\theta)}\)

\(= \dfrac{-1}{\tan\theta - \sec\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sec\theta - \tan\theta} = \) RHS

subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
context: In \(\triangle\)ABC, right-angled at B, AB \(= 24\) cm, BC \(= 7\) cm. Determine :
solution:
By Pythagoras theorem, \(\text{AC} = \sqrt{24^2 + 7^2} = \sqrt{576 + 49} = \sqrt{625} = 25\) cm.

For angle A, the opposite side is BC \(= 7\) and the adjacent side is AB \(= 24\).

\(\sin \text{A} = \dfrac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} = \dfrac{7}{25}\),  \(\cos \text{A} = \dfrac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}} = \dfrac{24}{25}\)

context: In \(\triangle\)ABC, right-angled at B, AB \(= 24\) cm, BC \(= 7\) cm. Determine :

For angle C, the opposite side is AB \(= 24\) and the adjacent side is BC \(= 7\).

\(\sin \text{C} = \dfrac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}} = \dfrac{24}{25}\),  \(\cos \text{C} = \dfrac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} = \dfrac{7}{25}\)

stem: Given \(\sec\theta = \dfrac{13}{12}\), calculate all other trigonometric ratios.
solution:

Take the adjacent side \(= 12k\) and the hypotenuse \(= 13k\). Then the opposite side is \(\sqrt{169k^2 - 144k^2} = 5k\).

subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
stem: If \(\angle\)A and \(\angle\)B are acute angles such that \(\cos \text{A} = \cos \text{B}\), then show that \(\angle\)A \(=\) \(\angle\)B.
solution:
Let \(\triangle\)ABC be a triangle right-angled at C, so that A and B are its two acute angles.

Then \(\cos \text{A} = \dfrac{\text{AC}}{\text{AB}}\) and \(\cos \text{B} = \dfrac{\text{BC}}{\text{AB}}\).

We are given \(\cos \text{A} = \cos \text{B}\), so

\(\dfrac{\text{AC}}{\text{AB}} = \dfrac{\text{BC}}{\text{AB}}\), which gives \(\text{AC} = \text{BC}\).

So the two legs of the right triangle are equal, making \(\triangle\)ABC isosceles.

The angles opposite equal sides are equal. The angle opposite AC is \(\angle\)B and the angle opposite BC is \(\angle\)A.

Therefore \(\angle\)A \(=\) \(\angle\)B.

subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
stem: In \(\triangle\)PQR, right-angled at Q, PR \(+\) QR \(= 25\) cm and PQ \(= 5\) cm. Determine the values of \(\sin \text{P}\), \(\cos \text{P}\) and \(\tan \text{P}\).
solution:
Let QR \(= x\) cm. Then PR \(= (25 - x)\) cm.

By Pythagoras theorem, \(\text{PR}^2 = \text{PQ}^2 + \text{QR}^2\):

\((25 - x)^2 = 5^2 + x^2\), i.e., \(625 - 50x + x^2 = 25 + x^2\), i.e., \(50x = 600\), so \(x = 12\).

So QR \(= 12\) cm and PR \(= 13\) cm.

\(\sin \text{P} = \dfrac{\text{QR}}{\text{PR}} = \dfrac{12}{13}\),  \(\cos \text{P} = \dfrac{\text{PQ}}{\text{PR}} = \dfrac{5}{13}\),  \(\tan \text{P} = \dfrac{\text{QR}}{\text{PQ}} = \dfrac{12}{5}\)

subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
context: If \(\cot\theta = \dfrac{7}{8}\), evaluate :
solution:
With \(\cot\theta = \dfrac{7}{8}\), take the adjacent side \(= 7k\) and the opposite side \(= 8k\); the hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{49k^2 + 64k^2} = k\sqrt{113}\).

So \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{8}{\sqrt{113}}\) and \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{7}{\sqrt{113}}\).

\(\dfrac{(1 + \sin\theta)(1 - \sin\theta)}{(1 + \cos\theta)(1 - \cos\theta)} = \dfrac{1 - \sin^2\theta}{1 - \cos^2\theta} = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin^2\theta} = \cot^2\theta\)

\(= \left(\dfrac{7}{8}\right)^2 = \dfrac{49}{64}\)

context: If \(\cot\theta = \dfrac{7}{8}\), evaluate :
solution: \(\cot^2\theta = \left(\dfrac{7}{8}\right)^2 = \dfrac{49}{64}\)

subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
context: In triangle ABC, right-angled at B, if \(\tan \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), find the value of:
solution:
Since \(\tan \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), we have \(\angle\)A \(= 30^\circ\), and since \(\angle\)B \(= 90^\circ\), \(\angle\)C \(= 60^\circ\).

So \(\sin \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\cos \text{A} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), \(\sin \text{C} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), \(\cos \text{C} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

\(\sin \text{A} \cos \text{C} + \cos \text{A} \sin \text{C} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4} = 1\)

subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
context: In triangle ABC, right-angled at B, if \(\tan \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), find the value of:
solution:
Since \(\tan \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), we have \(\angle\)A \(= 30^\circ\), and since \(\angle\)B \(= 90^\circ\), \(\angle\)C \(= 60^\circ\).

So \(\sin \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\cos \text{A} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), \(\sin \text{C} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), \(\cos \text{C} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

\(\cos \text{A} \cos \text{C} - \sin \text{A} \sin \text{C} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} = 0\)

subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
context: State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
stem: The value of \(\tan \text{A}\) is always less than 1.
solution:
**False.** \(\tan \text{A}\) can take any non-negative value for an acute angle.

For example, \(\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73 > 1\).

subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
context: State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
stem: \(\sec \text{A} = \dfrac{12}{5}\) for some value of angle A.
solution:
**True.** For an acute angle, \(\sec \text{A} = \dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{adjacent}} \ge 1\), and \(\dfrac{12}{5} = 2.4 \ge 1\).

A right triangle with adjacent side 5 and hypotenuse 12 exists (the third side is \(\sqrt{119}\)), so such an angle A exists.

subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
context: State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
stem: \(\cos \text{A}\) is the abbreviation used for the cosecant of angle A.
solution:
**False.** \(\cos \text{A}\) is the abbreviation for the **cosine** of angle A.

The cosecant is written \(\operatorname{cosec} \text{A}\).

subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
context: State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
stem: \(\cot \text{A}\) is the product of \(\cot\) and A.
solution:
**False.** \(\cot \text{A}\) is a single symbol denoting the cotangent of the angle A.

\(\cot\) has no meaning on its own, so it cannot be multiplied by A.

solution:

Since \(\dfrac{4}{3} > 1\), no such angle exists.

stem: If \(\tan(\text{A} + \text{B}) = \sqrt{3}\) and \(\tan(\text{A} - \text{B}) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\); \(0^\circ < \text{A} + \text{B} \le 90^\circ\); \(\text{A} > \text{B}\), find A and B.
solution:
Since \(\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}\) and \(0^\circ < \text{A} + \text{B} \le 90^\circ\), we get \(\text{A} + \text{B} = 60^\circ\)  ... (1)

Since \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), we get \(\text{A} - \text{B} = 30^\circ\)  ... (2)

Adding (1) and (2): \(2\text{A} = 90^\circ\), so \(\text{A} = 45^\circ\).

Subtracting (2) from (1): \(2\text{B} = 30^\circ\), so \(\text{B} = 15^\circ\).

context: State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
solution:
**False.** Take \(\text{A} = 30^\circ\) and \(\text{B} = 60^\circ\).

LHS \(= \sin 90^\circ = 1\), but RHS \(= \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \approx 1.37\).

Since one counterexample suffices, the statement is false.

context: State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
stem: The value of \(\sin\theta\) increases as \(\theta\) increases.
solution:
**True** (for \(0^\circ \le \theta \le 90^\circ\), the range in this chapter).

\(\sin 0^\circ = 0\), \(\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\sin 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), \(\sin 60^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), \(\sin 90^\circ = 1\) — the values rise steadily.

context: State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
stem: The value of \(\cos\theta\) increases as \(\theta\) increases.
solution:
**False.** \(\cos\theta\) **decreases** as \(\theta\) increases from \(0^\circ\) to \(90^\circ\).

\(\cos 0^\circ = 1\), \(\cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), \(\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\).

context: State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
solution:
**False.** They are equal only at \(\theta = 45^\circ\).

For example, at \(\theta = 30^\circ\), \(\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\) but \(\cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

context: State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answer.
solution:
**True.** \(\cot \text{A} = \dfrac{\cos \text{A}}{\sin \text{A}}\), and \(\sin 0^\circ = 0\).

Division by zero is undefined, so \(\cot 0^\circ\) is not defined.

stem: Express the trigonometric ratios \(\sin \text{A}\), \(\sec \text{A}\) and \(\tan \text{A}\) in terms of \(\cot \text{A}\).
solution:
We use \(\operatorname{cosec}^2 \text{A} = 1 + \cot^2 \text{A}\).

So \(\operatorname{cosec} \text{A} = \sqrt{1 + \cot^2 \text{A}}\) (positive for an acute angle), and therefore

\(\sin \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{\operatorname{cosec} \text{A}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \cot^2 \text{A}}}\)

\(\tan \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{\cot \text{A}}\)

\(\sec \text{A} = \sqrt{1 + \tan^2 \text{A}} = \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{1}{\cot^2 \text{A}}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{1 + \cot^2 \text{A}}}{\cot \text{A}}\)

stem: Write all the other trigonometric ratios of \(\angle\)A in terms of \(\sec \text{A}\).
solution:
We use \(\sec^2 \text{A} = 1 + \tan^2 \text{A}\), so \(\tan \text{A} = \sqrt{\sec^2 \text{A} - 1}\).

\(\cos \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{\sec \text{A}}\)

\(\tan \text{A} = \sqrt{\sec^2 \text{A} - 1}\)

\(\sin \text{A} = \tan \text{A} \cos \text{A} = \dfrac{\sqrt{\sec^2 \text{A} - 1}}{\sec \text{A}}\)

\(\cot \text{A} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\sec^2 \text{A} - 1}}\)

\(\operatorname{cosec} \text{A} = \dfrac{\sec \text{A}}{\sqrt{\sec^2 \text{A} - 1}}\)

context: Choose the correct option. Justify your choice.
solution:
\(9 \sec^2 \text{A} - 9 \tan^2 \text{A} = 9\left(\sec^2 \text{A} - \tan^2 \text{A}\right)\)

By the identity \(\sec^2 \text{A} = 1 + \tan^2 \text{A}\), we have \(\sec^2 \text{A} - \tan^2 \text{A} = 1\).

So the value is \(9 \times 1 = 9\).

So the answer is **(B)**.

context: Choose the correct option. Justify your choice.
solution:
Write everything in terms of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\):

\(= \left(1 + \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} + \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\right)\left(1 + \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} - \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}\right)\)

\(= \dfrac{(\cos\theta + \sin\theta + 1)(\sin\theta + \cos\theta - 1)}{\cos\theta \sin\theta}\)

The numerator is of the form \((p + 1)(p - 1) = p^2 - 1\) with \(p = \sin\theta + \cos\theta\):

\(= \dfrac{(\sin\theta + \cos\theta)^2 - 1}{\sin\theta \cos\theta} = \dfrac{\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta - 1}{\sin\theta \cos\theta}\)

\(= \dfrac{1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta - 1}{\sin\theta \cos\theta} = \dfrac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\sin\theta \cos\theta} = 2\)

So the answer is **(C)**.

context: Choose the correct option. Justify your choice.
solution:
\((\sec \text{A} + \tan \text{A})(1 - \sin \text{A}) = \left(\dfrac{1}{\cos \text{A}} + \dfrac{\sin \text{A}}{\cos \text{A}}\right)(1 - \sin \text{A})\)

\(= \dfrac{(1 + \sin \text{A})(1 - \sin \text{A})}{\cos \text{A}} = \dfrac{1 - \sin^2 \text{A}}{\cos \text{A}}\)

\(= \dfrac{\cos^2 \text{A}}{\cos \text{A}} = \cos \text{A}\)

So the answer is **(D)**.

context: Choose the correct option. Justify your choice.
solution:
\(1 + \tan^2 \text{A} = \sec^2 \text{A}\) and \(1 + \cot^2 \text{A} = \operatorname{cosec}^2 \text{A}\).

\(\dfrac{\sec^2 \text{A}}{\operatorname{cosec}^2 \text{A}} = \dfrac{1/\cos^2 \text{A}}{1/\sin^2 \text{A}} = \dfrac{\sin^2 \text{A}}{\cos^2 \text{A}} = \tan^2 \text{A}\)

So the answer is **(D)**.

context: Prove the following identities, where the angles involved are acute angles for which the expressions are defined.
solution:
LHS \(= \left(\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} - \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\right)^2 = \dfrac{(1 - \cos\theta)^2}{\sin^2\theta}\)

\(= \dfrac{(1 - \cos\theta)^2}{1 - \cos^2\theta} = \dfrac{(1 - \cos\theta)^2}{(1 - \cos\theta)(1 + \cos\theta)}\)

\(= \dfrac{1 - \cos\theta}{1 + \cos\theta} = \) RHS

context: Prove the following identities, where the angles involved are acute angles for which the expressions are defined.
solution:
LHS \(= \dfrac{\cos^2 \text{A} + (1 + \sin \text{A})^2}{(1 + \sin \text{A})\cos \text{A}}\)

\(= \dfrac{\cos^2 \text{A} + 1 + 2\sin \text{A} + \sin^2 \text{A}}{(1 + \sin \text{A})\cos \text{A}}\)

\(= \dfrac{1 + 1 + 2\sin \text{A}}{(1 + \sin \text{A})\cos \text{A}} = \dfrac{2(1 + \sin \text{A})}{(1 + \sin \text{A})\cos \text{A}}\)

\(= \dfrac{2}{\cos \text{A}} = 2 \sec \text{A} = \) RHS

context: Prove the following identities, where the angles involved are acute angles for which the expressions are defined.
stem:
\(\dfrac{\tan\theta}{1 - \cot\theta} + \dfrac{\cot\theta}{1 - \tan\theta} = 1 + \sec\theta \operatorname{cosec}\theta\)

[Hint : Write the expression in terms of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\)]
solution:
Write both terms in terms of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\):

\(\dfrac{\tan\theta}{1 - \cot\theta} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}}{1 - \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}} = \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)}\)

\(\dfrac{\cot\theta}{1 - \tan\theta} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}}{1 - \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}} = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta(\cos\theta - \sin\theta)}\)

So LHS \(= \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)} - \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)}\)

\(= \dfrac{\sin^3\theta - \cos^3\theta}{\sin\theta \cos\theta (\sin\theta - \cos\theta)}\)

Using \(a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)\):

\(= \dfrac{(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)(\sin^2\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta)}{\sin\theta \cos\theta (\sin\theta - \cos\theta)} = \dfrac{1 + \sin\theta\cos\theta}{\sin\theta \cos\theta}\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta \cos\theta} + 1 = 1 + \sec\theta \operatorname{cosec}\theta = \) RHS

context: Prove the following identities, where the angles involved are acute angles for which the expressions are defined.
solution:
LHS \(= \dfrac{1 + \sec \text{A}}{\sec \text{A}} = \dfrac{1 + \dfrac{1}{\cos \text{A}}}{\dfrac{1}{\cos \text{A}}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{\cos \text{A} + 1}{\cos \text{A}}}{\dfrac{1}{\cos \text{A}}} = 1 + \cos \text{A}\)

RHS \(= \dfrac{\sin^2 \text{A}}{1 - \cos \text{A}} = \dfrac{1 - \cos^2 \text{A}}{1 - \cos \text{A}} = \dfrac{(1 - \cos \text{A})(1 + \cos \text{A})}{1 - \cos \text{A}} = 1 + \cos \text{A}\)

LHS \(=\) RHS, so the identity holds.

context: Prove the following identities, where the angles involved are acute angles for which the expressions are defined.
solution:
Divide the numerator and denominator of the LHS by \(\sin \text{A}\):

LHS \(= \dfrac{\cot \text{A} - 1 + \operatorname{cosec} \text{A}}{\cot \text{A} + 1 - \operatorname{cosec} \text{A}}\)

\(= \dfrac{(\cot \text{A} + \operatorname{cosec} \text{A}) - 1}{(\cot \text{A} - \operatorname{cosec} \text{A}) + 1}\)

Multiply numerator and denominator by \((\cot \text{A} - \operatorname{cosec} \text{A})\):

\(= \dfrac{\left[(\cot \text{A} + \operatorname{cosec} \text{A}) - 1\right](\cot \text{A} - \operatorname{cosec} \text{A})}{\left[(\cot \text{A} - \operatorname{cosec} \text{A}) + 1\right](\cot \text{A} - \operatorname{cosec} \text{A})}\)

The numerator becomes \((\cot^2 \text{A} - \operatorname{cosec}^2 \text{A}) - (\cot \text{A} - \operatorname{cosec} \text{A}) = -1 - \cot \text{A} + \operatorname{cosec} \text{A}\),

using \(\operatorname{cosec}^2 \text{A} = 1 + \cot^2 \text{A}\).

So LHS \(= \dfrac{-\left(1 + \cot \text{A} - \operatorname{cosec} \text{A}\right)}{\left(\cot \text{A} - \operatorname{cosec} \text{A} + 1\right)(\cot \text{A} - \operatorname{cosec} \text{A})}\)

\(= \dfrac{-1}{\cot \text{A} - \operatorname{cosec} \text{A}} = \dfrac{1}{\operatorname{cosec} \text{A} - \cot \text{A}}\)

Multiplying numerator and denominator by \((\operatorname{cosec} \text{A} + \cot \text{A})\) and using \(\operatorname{cosec}^2 \text{A} - \cot^2 \text{A} = 1\):

\(= \operatorname{cosec} \text{A} + \cot \text{A} = \) RHS

context: Prove the following identities, where the angles involved are acute angles for which the expressions are defined.
solution:
Multiply inside the square root by \(\dfrac{1 + \sin \text{A}}{1 + \sin \text{A}}\):

LHS \(= \sqrt{\dfrac{(1 + \sin \text{A})^2}{(1 - \sin \text{A})(1 + \sin \text{A})}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{(1 + \sin \text{A})^2}{1 - \sin^2 \text{A}}}\)

\(= \sqrt{\dfrac{(1 + \sin \text{A})^2}{\cos^2 \text{A}}} = \dfrac{1 + \sin \text{A}}{\cos \text{A}}\)

(the positive root, since A is acute)

\(= \dfrac{1}{\cos \text{A}} + \dfrac{\sin \text{A}}{\cos \text{A}} = \sec \text{A} + \tan \text{A} = \) RHS

context: Prove the following identities, where the angles involved are acute angles for which the expressions are defined.
solution:
Factor \(\sin\theta\) from the numerator and \(\cos\theta\) from the denominator:

LHS \(= \dfrac{\sin\theta\left(1 - 2\sin^2\theta\right)}{\cos\theta\left(2\cos^2\theta - 1\right)}\)

Now \(1 - 2\sin^2\theta = 1 - 2(1 - \cos^2\theta) = 2\cos^2\theta - 1\).

So the bracketed factors are equal and cancel:

\(= \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta = \) RHS

context: Prove the following identities, where the angles involved are acute angles for which the expressions are defined.
solution:
Expand both squares:

LHS \(= \sin^2 \text{A} + 2\sin \text{A}\operatorname{cosec} \text{A} + \operatorname{cosec}^2 \text{A} + \cos^2 \text{A} + 2\cos \text{A}\sec \text{A} + \sec^2 \text{A}\)

Since \(\sin \text{A}\operatorname{cosec} \text{A} = 1\) and \(\cos \text{A}\sec \text{A} = 1\),

\(= \left(\sin^2 \text{A} + \cos^2 \text{A}\right) + 2 + 2 + \operatorname{cosec}^2 \text{A} + \sec^2 \text{A}\)

\(= 1 + 4 + \left(1 + \cot^2 \text{A}\right) + \left(1 + \tan^2 \text{A}\right)\)

\(= 7 + \tan^2 \text{A} + \cot^2 \text{A} = \) RHS
